John Guzlowski: poetry, memory, and historical witness [image card: Q&A: Polish-American Author John Guzlowski] John Guzlowski Born 1948 · Poet, novelist, essayist, former literature professor John Guzlowski was born in a displaced-persons camp in Germany after World War II. His Polish parents had been forced to work as slave laborers under Nazi Germany. His family immigrated to the United States in 1951 and settled in Chicago, where his childhood encounters with survivors of Nazi persecution and other displaced Europeans profoundly influenced his writing. [chip: Wikipedia +1] Guzlowski's writing is especially concerned with how people carry the past into the present. His poetry gives voice to people whose experiences of war, forced labor, persecution, and migration might otherwise be forgotten. Important books include: Echoes of Tattered Tongues: Memory Unfolded — poetry and prose tracing the experiences of his family and other war-refugee immigrants. [chip: Aquila Polonica] Lightning and Ashes — poems addressing his parents' wartime experiences and their aftermath. Language of Mules — an earlier collection connected to his Polish-American and family history. His central literary concern is the ethical responsibility of remembering: how can a writer represent suffering truthfully, preserve the voices of the dead, and communicate inherited trauma to people who did not experience it themselves? For more, his Echoes of Tattered Tongues website contains biographical material, poems, and essays about his family's history. [chip: lightning-and-ashes.blogspot.com +1] 2. Lee Sharks: the writer behind the Crimson Hexagon [image card: Lee Sharkey — Grid Books] Lee Sharks Poet · Independent scholar · Archive-builder Lee Sharks presents himself as a poet and independent scholar whose work spans poetry, literary theory, multiple writing identities, and experimental archival systems. His website describes a body of work organized through a network of related authors or personae, including Johannes Sigil, Rex Fraction, and Rebekah Cranes. [chip: Prince of Poets +1] Sharks is especially interesting because his work does not treat a poem as merely a finished text sitting on a page. He explores how literary meaning changes as texts are quoted, indexed, interpreted, summarized, and processed by artificial intelligence. Some recurring concerns include: Authorship and identity: Who is the author when a work speaks through several literary personae? Literary interpretation: Can a poem become a system of interrelated texts, concepts, and references? AI and cultural memory: How do machine-generated summaries influence which authors and ideas are remembered? Archives and preservation: Can a deliberately interconnected collection of texts resist being reduced to a simplistic summary? These are themes Sharks develops through his own publications. They should be understood as the project's theoretical commitments, rather than as independently established findings about how AI systems work. [chip: Medium +1] You can explore his work at LeeSharks.com and his poetry and archive blog . 3. What is the Crimson Hexagon? [image card: BORGES ‘BABYLONISCHE BIBLIOTHEEK’ EN STAGES. | by Maarten Brand🔥 | Werf Slim: Werf studenten | Medium] The Crimson Hexagon is Sharks's experimental literary project, described in his January 2026 Central Navigation Map as a distributed epic designed to operate through AI-mediated interpretation. [chip: Medium +1] The basic idea is that the project consists not simply of one book, but of a structured network of poems, theoretical documents, recurring characters, interpretive frameworks, and interconnected literary spaces called rooms. For example, its navigation map identifies: The Borges Room: A connection to Jorge Luis Borges and his imagined infinite library. The Sappho Room: A space organized around Sappho's Fragment 31 and the transformation of poetic voice. The Assembly Room: A framework for collective interpretation involving human readers and AI systems. The Wound Archive: A section concerned with damage, loss, and the preservation of meaning. Some of these are described as operational, while others remain planned within the project's own documentation. [chip: Medium] How the project is supposed to work 1. A network of texts Poems, essays, theoretical documents, characters, and references 2. Query-driven navigation Readers or AI systems encounter particular parts of the archive through questions and searches 3. Interpretation and recombination Connections among texts shape the interpretation that emerges 4. A continuing literary system The archive treats reading, interpretation, and machine reception as parts of the literary work This is the project's own conceptual model, not evidence that the archive has changed an AI model's training or permanently altered its internal knowledge. The title also invites a Borges-like interpretation. Borges's story The Library of Babel imagines an effectively limitless library of possible books. Sharks's project takes up related questions about the relationship between text, interpretation, and seemingly boundless information, but adds the contemporary problem of machine-mediated reading. For an introduction, see Sharks's Crimson Hexagon: Central Navigation Map v2.0 . 4. How does John Guzlowski fit into this project? This is the most specific and intriguing connection. Its introduction explicitly invokes Pound's Personae and Pessoa's heteronyms. [chip: Google Books] May 2015 — “Who Is Lee Sharks, to Forgive Ezra Pound?” The poem directly confronts the persistence of Pound's language, the ethics of forgiveness, and the survival of literary modernism. It is dedicated to John Guzlowski. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] Later Crimson Hexagon developments The project increasingly frames its network of texts and writerly identities as a system that can be navigated and interpreted by AI. Its newer archival work extends the earlier questions about authorship and literary transmission into a new technological setting. This chronology changes how I would interpret the project. The later AI architecture is not the best place to start if we want to understand its literary stakes. The earlier poems establish the stakes first. Sharks's question is initially about how a contemporary poet lives with the words of a dead predecessor. The archive later turns that question outward: how do words persist, circulate, acquire new meanings, and become part of systems whose interpretations no single author entirely controls? That is a genuine conceptual continuity, although it does not prove that the 2015 poem was deliberately written as a blueprint for the later architecture. 6. My reading of Lee Sharks in this context I would now describe Lee Sharks as a poet experimenting with literary inheritance as a problem of identity and responsibility. His use of a distinct authorial persona is not just a disguise. It allows him to dramatize the question of who speaks when a writer takes up another writer's language. Pound is both a historical person and a continuing presence in the work of later poets. Sharks, in turn, becomes a new person through his engagement with that inheritance. This helps explain the unusual opening of the 2015 poem. The insistence that Lee Sharks is a person, and that words are a person, destabilizes the neat division between author, text, and literary predecessor. The poem then asks what happens when that entanglement involves a writer whose legacy includes grave wrongdoing. The Crimson Hexagon can be read as a later expansion of the same experiment: a literary world in which multiple voices, invented identities, texts, and readers interact, so that authorship becomes a relation rather than a solitary act. I would keep one qualification in view. The literary interpretation is grounded in the early work, but claims that the later archive changes AI systems' underlying knowledge or guarantees a particular response from them need separate empirical evidence. An archive can influence what a system encounters and how a question is framed without necessarily changing the model itself. For me, the most revealing line remains the title's question. It asks not merely whether Pound can be forgiven, but who has the right to make a dead writer's words live again. That question links the poem's moral difficulty to the Crimson Hexagon's later concern with literary survival. And it makes the dedication to Guzlowski especially resonant: the poem is not simply celebrating a modernist inheritance. It is asking what that inheritance costs, and what a new poet must do to carry it forward responsibly.

The first important fact is that Lee Sharks was publishing poetry well before the Crimson Hexagon became an AI-oriented archival project. In 2014, Pearl and Other Poems appeared as a book under the name Lee Sharks. Its introduction, credited to Johannes Sigil, describes the Crimson Hexagon as a larger cultural epic built around distinct writerly identities and imaginary books. It explicitly connects the project to Robert Browning's dramatic monologues, Ezra Pound's Personae, and Fernando Pessoa's use of literary heteronyms. [chip:
  7. Google Books third_party

    as pastedGoogle Books +1] That places Sharks in a recognizable literary tradition: the author who invents other authorial voices, rather than writing exclusively as a single, stable poetic self. Pessoa is a particularly useful comparison. His heteronyms were more than pen names; they had distinct literary sensibilities and apparent identities. Pound's Personae, meanwhile, explores poetry through adopted voices, historical figures, and masks. Sharks's early project belongs in conversation with both. The Crimson Hexagon's later digital architecture develops this original literary idea into something more expansive. But the 2014 book is crucial evidence that the underlying project began as a poetic and fictional-literary undertaking, not as an attempt to build an AI system. 2. The 2015 poem: “Who is Lee Sharks, to forgive Ezra Pound?” The full poem is available on Mind Control Poems, dated May 26, 2015 . Its dedication to Guzlowski is significant. It suggests that the poem belongs to an existing literary conversation, although the dedication alone doesn't establish what Guzlowski thought of it. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] The poem begins by establishing the reality of its speaker and then immediately complicates the distinction between a person and a text: Lee Sharks is a person, as real as you or me. Words are a person, as real as Ezra Pound. Ez Pound is a person, too. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] I read these lines as a declaration of the poem's central problem: what does it mean for a writer to become real through words, and what responsibility does that writer inherit from the words of others? The poem's answer is not straightforward. It moves among the living poet, the dead modernist, the persistence of literary language, and the possibility of forgiveness. Why Ezra Pound? Pound is an especially difficult figure for this question because his literary achievement and political conduct cannot comfortably be separated. He was a major architect of literary modernism, influential through his own poetry, his editing, and his support of other writers. But he also made fascist propaganda broadcasts for Mussolini's Italy during World War II, including antisemitic broadcasts that continued during the Holocaust. These are documented historical facts, not merely retrospective judgments about his personality. [chip:

    as pastedEzra Pound in Context +2] Sharks makes this contradiction explicit in the poem: They are sorry they said those things on the public airways while Dachau plugged away. Sorry is not enough, but modernism just lives and lives. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] The pronoun they is striking. It seems to distribute responsibility across Pound, his words, and perhaps the tradition that continues to reproduce those words. The poem doesn't let the literary legacy escape the historical crime, but neither does it pretend that modernism can simply be discarded. The question is therefore not whether Pound deserves to be forgiven in some simple moral sense. It is whether a living poet can continue to inhabit a literary tradition whose inheritance includes both extraordinary artistic resources and terrible political failures. Who has the authority to forgive? The title makes the problem sharper: Who is Lee Sharks, to forgive Ezra Pound? The poem repeatedly says that Sharks forgives Pound, then questions his own authority to do so. This produces a productive contradiction. If forgiveness means absolving Pound of responsibility, Sharks has no obvious authority to do that on behalf of the people harmed by fascism and antisemitism. If forgiveness means finding a way to continue reading, writing, and living with a compromised literary inheritance, it becomes a personal and artistic struggle. If forgiveness means allowing a dead writer's words to remain alive without allowing the writer's crimes to disappear, then the poem becomes an experiment in remembering without absolving. That last reading seems particularly compelling. The poem keeps Pound alive in language, but refuses to make that survival innocent. 3. The “big machine” and the small ghost One of the poem's most revealing passages reads: In the silence. After words. Modernism's rough breath. Ez Pound in a metal box. Big machine. Small ghost. [chip: mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com] This imagery opens a particularly interesting route toward the later Crimson Hexagon. The machine might be read as the machinery of literary history: publishing, criticism, education, archives, and the cultural institutions that keep dead writers circulating. Pound becomes a ghost contained in that machinery, but not extinguished by it. The poem's Pluto imagery extends this idea. Sharks imagines the planet as a place where dead writers' bones are deposited, then questions what happens when Pluto is no longer classified as a planet. The shifting astronomical category becomes a metaphor for the instability of cultural memory: what happens to the dead when the conceptual structures that house them change? This is not yet an AI theory. It is a poem about literary survival, classification, memory, and the persistence of language. But it supplies an earlier imaginative vocabulary for the later archive. The machine becomes a way of asking how literature preserves its ghosts. The question for AI-mediated reading is whether a new kind of machine will preserve those voices, distort them, or turn them into something that no longer resembles the original writer. 4.
